markdown.markdown:
SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) remains one of the most widely used
mechanisms for retrieving status and operational information from network devices.

In this lab, we will use a MikroTik router as the managed device and Python to
develop simple network management and monitoring tools.

The lab follows a progression similar to that used by real network management
platforms:

1. **Discover** which devices are present in the network.
2. **Identify** which devices can be managed using SNMP.
3. **Inspect** the information exposed by those devices.
4. **Explore** their interfaces and other objects available through their MIBs.
5. **Monitor** how selected network parameters evolve over time.

Throughout the lab, you will work directly from a Linux system and use both
command-line tools and Python scripts.

# Learning Objectives

After completing this lab, you should be able to:

- prepare a Python environment on Linux for developing simple network management
  tools;
- understand the relationship between **OIDs**, **MIBs**, scalar objects, and tables;
- perform SNMP queries using `GET`, `GETNEXT`, and `WALK`;
- interpret SNMP responses and the `VarBind` structures exchanged between manager
  and agent;
- modify managed objects using `SET` when permitted by the agent;
- automatically discover devices on a network and determine which of them provide
  SNMP management;
- retrieve and interpret the interface table of a network device;
- use SNMP counters to calculate traffic rates;
- develop a simple interface monitor using Python;
- understand the fundamental differences between SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3.

# Lab Environment

Each student has an individual laboratory environment accessible through the
CyberRange.

The lab will mainly use two systems:

- a **Debian container**, from which command-line tools and Python scripts will
  be executed;
- a **MikroTik router**, which will act as the SNMP agent and the network device
  being monitored.

The basic architecture is:

```text
┌──────────────────────┐
│      Debian CT       │
│                      │
│  Python / pysnmp     │
│  snmpget / snmpwalk  │
│  tcpdump             │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           │
           │ SNMP
           ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│      MikroTik        │
│                      │
│     SNMP Agent       │
│       MIB-II         │
└──────────────────────┘
````

# Preparing the Environment

In previous labs, the programming environment and the required Python libraries
may have been provided preconfigured. In this course, you will prepare your own
working environment.

This is a common task when deploying network management and observability tools:
before collecting telemetry, you need a system from which to run them.

## Accessing the Debian Container

Connect to your **Debian container (d13-basic-153)** through the CyberRange and open a terminal.

Check the operating system and the installed Python version:

```bash
cat /etc/os-release
python3 --version
```

Throughout this lab, the Debian container will act as the **SNMP manager**, while
the MikroTik router will act as the **SNMP agent**.

::: {.callout-note}
### Manager and agent

An **SNMP manager** sends requests to managed devices and processes their
responses.

An **SNMP agent** runs on the managed device and provides access to the
management information exposed by that device.
:::

## Installing SNMP Command-Line Tools

Before writing Python programs, we will verify SNMP communication using standard
Linux command-line tools.

Update the package information and install the SNMP utilities:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install snmp
```

Check that the tools are available:

```bash
snmpget --version
```

Some of the commands that we will use during this lab are:

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `snmpget` | Retrieve one or more specific objects |
| `snmpgetnext` | Retrieve the next object in the MIB tree |
| `snmpwalk` | Traverse a subtree of the MIB |
| `snmpset` | Modify a writable object |

Do not worry about their complete syntax yet. We will introduce each command
when it is needed.

Python projects commonly use **virtual environments** to keep their dependencies

Install the required package if it is not already available:

```bash
mkdir ~/p1-snmp
cd ~/p1-snmp
```

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
```

Activate it:

::: {.callout-tip}
Whenever you start a new terminal and return to this lab, activate the

## Installing PySNMP

With the virtual environment activated, install PySNMP:

```bash
pip install pysnmp
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
python3 -c "import pysnmp; print(pysnmp.__version__)"
```

## Checking Network Connectivity

Before using SNMP, verify that the MikroTik router is reachable from your Debian
container.

```bash
ping -c 3 <MIKROTIK_IP>
```

Replace `<MIKROTIK_IP>` with the IP address assigned to the MikroTik router in
your laboratory environment.

::: {.callout-important}
Being able to reach a device using ICMP does **not** imply that the device
supports SNMP. Similarly, a device that does not reply to ICMP Echo Requests
could still provide other network services.

We will revisit this distinction when implementing automatic device discovery.
:::

```text

│
├── Linux SNMP tools
│   ├── snmpget
│   ├── snmpgetnext
│   ├── snmpwalk
│   └── snmpset

```

# First Contact with SNMP

We now have the tools required to act as an SNMP manager. The next step is to
configure the MikroTik router as an SNMP agent and perform our first query.

## Configuring the MikroTik SNMP Agent

Connect to your MikroTik router and verify the SNMP configuration.

Enable the SNMP agent if necessary and configure the following community:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| SNMP version | SNMPv2c |
| Community | `public` |
| Access | Read-only |

::: {.callout-warning}
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c communities are transmitted without encryption and should
not be considered secure authentication mechanisms.

We use SNMPv2c here because it allows us to focus first on the SNMP data model
and protocol operations. SNMPv3 will be introduced later in the lab.
:::

## Your First SNMP GET

Let's retrieve `sysDescr.0` from the MikroTik.

`sysDescr` belongs to the `system` group of MIB-II and contains a textual
description of the managed device.

Its numeric OID is:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

From the Debian container, execute:

```bash
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

You should obtain a response similar to:

```text
iso.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 = STRING: ...
```

The exact value depends on your MikroTik router.

Notice that the result contains three different pieces of information:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0  =  STRING  :  value
        │                  │         │
        │                  │         └── Object value
        │                  │
        │                  └──────────── ASN.1 data type
        │
        └─────────────────────────────── Object identifier
```

This `(OID, value)` association is the basic information carried by an SNMP
**VarBind**.

::: {.callout-note}
### Why does the OID end in `.0`?

`sysDescr` is a scalar object.

SNMP identifies an **instance** of a scalar object by appending `.0` to the
object OID. Therefore, a GET request must use the complete instance OID:

```text
sysDescr.0
```

Later, when working with tables, the suffix will have a different meaning:
it will identify a particular row of the table.
:::

## Exploring the `system` Group

The `system` group is located below:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1
```

Use `snmpwalk` to retrieve the objects available below this OID:

```bash
snmpwalk -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1
```

Identify at least the following objects in the output:

| Object | Information |
|---|---|
| `sysDescr` | Device description |
| `sysObjectID` | Type of managed device |
| `sysUpTime` | Time since the management system was initialized |
| `sysContact` | Contact information |
| `sysName` | Device name |
| `sysLocation` | Physical/location information |
| `sysServices` | Services provided by the device |

::: {.callout-question}
Compare `sysDescr` and `sysObjectID`.

What type of information does each object provide? Why could `sysObjectID`
be particularly useful for an automatic network management system?
:::

## Looking at the Protocol

So far, the `snmpget` command has hidden the actual SNMP message exchange.

Capture the traffic generated by a single GET operation using the packet
capture mechanism provided in the laboratory environment.

Start the capture and execute again:

```bash
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

Stop the capture after receiving the response and inspect the SNMP packets.

You should find two messages:

```text
Debian CT                              MikroTik
(manager)                              (agent)

    │                                     │
    │ ----------- GET request ----------> │
    │                                     │
    │ <---------- RESPONSE -------------- │
    │                                     │
```

Inspect the GET request and answer the following questions:

1. Which SNMP version is being used?
2. Can you find the community string in the packet?
3. Which OID appears in the VarBind?
4. What value is included in the VarBind of the GET request?
5. Find the corresponding VarBind in the response. What has changed?

::: {.callout-important}
Do not capture and analyse dozens of packets. The objective is to understand
**one request and its corresponding response**.

You should be able to relate what you see in the packet capture to the SNMP
manager/agent model studied in class.
:::

## Performing the Same GET with Python

The command-line tools are useful for testing and troubleshooting, but our goal
is to build network management software.

Create a file named:

```text
get_system.py
```

Using PySNMP, retrieve `sysDescr.0` from your MikroTik router.

Your program should display:

```text
OID:   ...
Type:  ...
Value: ...
```

::: {.callout-tip}
At this point, focus on understanding the PySNMP operation rather than building

Identify in your program:

- the SNMP version;
- the community;
- the address of the agent;
- the requested OID;
- the returned VarBind.
:::

Once the program works, compare its result with the one obtained using
`snmpget`.

Both tools are acting as SNMP managers and should retrieve the same managed
object from the same agent.

# GET Operations and VarBinds

In the previous section, you retrieved a single managed object using an SNMP
GET operation.

An SNMP GET request, however, can contain **more than one VarBind**. This allows
a manager to request several objects using a single SNMP message.

In this section, we will compare both approaches and examine how SNMP handles
errors.

## A Minimal PySNMP Example

PySNMP provides an asynchronous API based on Python's `asyncio`.

The following example retrieves `sysUpTime.0` from an SNMP agent:

```python
import asyncio

from pysnmp.hlapi.v3arch.asyncio import (
    SnmpEngine,
    CommunityData,
    UdpTransportTarget,
    ContextData,
    ObjectType,
    ObjectIdentity,
    get_cmd,
)


async def main():
    target = await UdpTransportTarget.create(
        ("<MIKROTIK_IP>", 161)
    )

    error_indication, error_status, error_index, var_binds = await get_cmd(
        SnmpEngine(),
        CommunityData("public", mpModel=1),
        target,
        ContextData(),
        ObjectType(ObjectIdentity("1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0")),
    )

    if error_indication:
        print(error_indication)
    elif error_status:
        print(
            f"{error_status.prettyPrint()} at "
            f"{error_index and var_binds[int(error_index) - 1][0] or '?'}"
        )
    else:
        for oid, value in var_binds:
            print("OID:  ", oid.prettyPrint())
            print("Type: ", type(value).__name__)
            print("Value:", value.prettyPrint())


asyncio.run(main())
```

Replace `<MIKROTIK_IP>` with the address of your MikroTik router and execute the
program.

::: {.callout-question}
Before continuing, identify in the program:

- where the SNMP agent is specified;
- where the UDP port is specified;
- where the community is specified;
- where SNMPv2c is selected;
- where the requested OID is specified;
- where the program waits for the SNMP response;
- which variable contains the returned VarBinds.

Why is `await` appropriate for an operation such as an SNMP request?
:::

## What Happens When an Object Does Not Exist?

We will now examine how SNMP handles errors.

Create a GET request containing several valid objects from the `system` group
and one OID that does not exist.

For example, you may deliberately modify one of the valid OIDs.

First perform the request using **SNMPv1**.

In PySNMP, SNMPv1 can be selected using:

```python
CommunityData("public", mpModel=0)
```

Record:

- `error_indication`;
- `error_status`;
- `error_index`;
- the returned VarBinds.

Now repeat exactly the same request using **SNMPv2c**:

```python
CommunityData("public", mpModel=1)
```

Compare the results.

::: {.callout-question}
### SNMPv1 vs SNMPv2c

1. What happens to the complete request when one of the requested objects does
   not exist in SNMPv1?
2. Can you determine which VarBind caused the error?
3. What happens with SNMPv2c?
4. Are the valid objects still returned?
5. How is the nonexistent object represented?

Explain why the SNMPv2c behaviour is more useful when a manager requests
several objects in a single operation.
:::

## Sequential Requests vs Concurrent Requests

Experiment 1 deliberately performed the seven GET operations sequentially:

```text
GET 1 → wait → GET 2 → wait → GET 3 → wait → ...
```

However, SNMP requests are primarily **I/O-bound operations**: most of the time
the program is waiting for network responses.

Create a third version in which the seven individual GET operations are
started concurrently using `asyncio.gather()`.

Conceptually:

```python
results = await asyncio.gather(
    get_one(OID_1),
    get_one(OID_2),
    get_one(OID_3),
    # ...
)
```

Measure the execution time.

You now have three different strategies:

| Strategy | SNMP requests | Execution |
|---|---:|---|
| Individual GETs | 7 | Sequential |
| Multiple VarBinds | 1 | Single request |
| Individual GETs + `gather()` | 7 | Concurrent |

::: {.callout-question}
Compare the three measured times.

Why can concurrent individual GETs be significantly faster than sequential
GETs even though both approaches generate the same number of SNMP messages?

Does concurrency eliminate the network overhead of sending multiple SNMP
requests?

Which of the three approaches would you choose for retrieving several objects
from **one device**? Would your answer necessarily be the same if you were
monitoring **many different devices**?
:::

::: {.callout-note}
This distinction will become important later in the lab.

When monitoring a single device, grouping several objects into one SNMP request
can reduce protocol overhead.

When monitoring many independent devices, asynchronous execution allows the
manager to communicate with several agents without waiting for each operation
to finish before starting the next one.
:::

# Navigating the MIB: GETNEXT and WALK

So far, every GET operation required the manager to know the exact OID of the
object to retrieve.

But what happens if the manager does not know all the objects available below
a particular OID?

SNMP provides the `GETNEXT` operation for this purpose.

## Using GETNEXT

A GETNEXT request does not ask for the value of the specified OID itself.
Instead, it asks the agent for the **next OID in lexicographical order**.

For example, consider part of the MIB-II `system` subtree:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1
│
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0   sysDescr.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0   sysObjectID.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0   sysUpTime.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0   sysContact.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0   sysName.0
└── ...
```

If the manager asks for the object following:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

the agent should return:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0
```

Try it from the command line:

```bash
snmpgetnext -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

Now try:

```bash
snmpgetnext -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0
```

and observe the returned OID.

::: {.callout-question}
What information must the manager know to perform a GET?

What information must it know to perform a GETNEXT?

Why can GETNEXT be useful when the manager does not know the complete contents
of a MIB subtree?
:::

## Building a WALK from GETNEXT

There is no `WALK` PDU in the SNMP protocol.

An SNMP walk is obtained by repeatedly asking the agent for the next object:

```text
start OID
    │
    ▼
 GETNEXT
    │
    ▼
returned OID ───┐
                │
                ▼
             GETNEXT
                │
                ▼
          returned OID ───┐
                          │
                         ...
```

The OID returned by one request becomes the starting OID for the next request.

The process continues until the returned OID no longer belongs to the subtree
being explored.

# Working with SNMP Tables

Scalar objects such as `sysName.0` represent a single value.

Network management, however, frequently involves collections of similar
objects. A router may have many interfaces, routes, neighbours, or addresses.

SNMP represents this type of information using **tables**.

## The Interface Table

MIB-II provides information about the network interfaces of a device below the
`interfaces` subtree:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.2
```

Explore it:

```bash
snmpwalk -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.2
```

The interface table contains information such as:

| Object | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ifIndex` | Interface identifier |
| `ifDescr` | Interface description |
| `ifType` | Interface type |
| `ifMtu` | Maximum transmission unit |
| `ifSpeed` | Estimated interface bandwidth |
| `ifPhysAddress` | Physical address |
| `ifAdminStatus` | Desired interface state |
| `ifOperStatus` | Current operational state |
| `ifInOctets` | Received octets |
| `ifOutOctets` | Transmitted octets |

Unlike scalar objects, table objects have an **index** identifying the row.

For example:

```text
ifDescr.1 = "ether1"
ifDescr.2 = "ether2"
ifDescr.3 = "ether3"
```

can be understood as:

```text
             ifIndex

               1        2        3
               │        │        │
               ▼        ▼        ▼

ifDescr      ether1   ether2   ether3
ifType       ...      ...      ...
ifSpeed      ...      ...      ...
ifOperStatus ...      ...      ...
ifInOctets   ...      ...      ...
ifOutOctets  ...      ...      ...
```

The index therefore connects values belonging to the **same interface**.

# From Counters to Telemetry

In the previous section, you observed that `ifInOctets` and `ifOutOctets` are
**cumulative counters**.

They do not directly tell us the current traffic rate of an interface.

To obtain a rate, the manager must sample a counter at different times and
calculate how much it has changed.

## From a Counter to a Rate

Suppose that the value of `ifInOctets` is measured at two different times:

| Time | Counter |
|---|---:|
| $t_1$ | $C_1$ |
| $t_2$ | $C_2$ |

The average incoming traffic rate during that interval is:

$$
R_{\text{in}} =
8 \frac{C_2-C_1}{t_2-t_1}
$$

where:

- $C_1$ and $C_2$ are counter values in octets;
- $t_1$ and $t_2$ are measured in seconds;
- the factor 8 converts octets into bits;
- $R_{\text{in}}$ is expressed in bit/s.

The same calculation can be applied to `ifOutOctets`.

::: {.callout-important}
SNMP does not calculate the traffic rate for us.

The agent exposes a **counter**. The manager samples that counter and derives
the **rate**.

This distinction between a raw measurement and a derived metric is fundamental
in network monitoring and observability.
:::

## Counter Size Matters

The original MIB-II interface table defines:

```text
ifInOctets
ifOutOctets
```

as 32-bit counters.

A 32-bit unsigned counter can represent values from:

$$
0
\quad\text{to}\quad
2^{32}-1
$$

After reaching its maximum value, the counter wraps around.

Consider a continuously busy **1 Gbit/s** interface.

::: {.callout-question}
Calculate approximately how long it would take a 32-bit octet counter to wrap
around at 1 Gbit/s.

5 minutes?
:::

For higher-capacity interfaces, IF-MIB provides 64-bit counters:

```text
ifHCInOctets
ifHCOutOctets
```

where **HC** stands for *High Capacity*.

Whenever they are available, these counters are generally preferable for
traffic monitoring.

::: {.callout-note}
A robust monitoring application should not simply assume that:

```text
new_counter >= old_counter
```

A counter may become smaller because of:

- counter wraparound;
- device or interface restart;
- agent restart.

Production monitoring systems must account for these situations.
:::

# Automatic Device Discovery

Until now, we have assumed that the network manager already knows the IP
address of the device to monitor.

In a real network management system, this information may not be known in
advance. Management platforms therefore provide **device discovery** mechanisms
to find devices and build an inventory automatically.

A simplified discovery process can be represented as:

```text
          Network
             │
             ▼
      Discover hosts
             │
             ▼
       IP + MAC address
             │
             ▼
        Probe SNMP
             │
        ┌────┴────┐
        │         │
       No        Yes
                  │
                  ▼
             Identify device
                  │
                  ▼
       sysName / sysDescr /
          sysObjectID
                  │
                  ▼
          Device inventory
```

In this section, you will implement a simplified version of this process.

## Discovering Hosts on a Local Network

If the manager is directly connected to an IPv4 LAN, **ARP** provides a useful
mechanism for discovering active hosts.

The manager can send an ARP request asking:

```text
Who has 192.168.153.1?
Who has 192.168.153.2?
Who has 192.168.153.3?
...
```

A device using one of those addresses can reply with its MAC address:

```text
Manager                                  Device

   │                                       │
   │── ARP: Who has 192.168.153.10? ─────>│
   │                                       │
   │<── ARP: 192.168.153.10 is at MAC ────│
   │                                       │
```

This provides two useful pieces of inventory information:

```text
IP address  ↔  MAC address
```

::: {.callout-note}
ARP discovery only works for devices in the same Layer-2 broadcast domain.

Routers do not normally forward ARP requests. Therefore, a management platform
cannot use ARP alone to discover arbitrary remote networks.
:::

## ARP Discovery with Scapy

For this experiment, we will use **Scapy**, a Python library for creating,
sending, receiving, and inspecting network packets.

We will only use a very small part of Scapy. The objective of this lab is not
to learn the complete library, but to use it to implement the discovery
mechanism discussed above.


### Building Packets with Scapy

Scapy represents network protocols as Python objects.

For example:

```python
from scapy.all import ARP

packet = ARP(
    pdst="192.168.153.10"
)
```

creates an ARP packet asking about the IPv4 address `192.168.153.10`.

You can inspect the packet using:

```python

```

Try it.

- sender protocol address (`psrc`);
- target hardware address (`hwdst`).

What values has Scapy automatically selected for the fields that you did not
specify?
:::

### Ethernet and ARP

ARP requests are transmitted inside Ethernet frames.

An ARP request intended for all hosts on the LAN therefore uses the Ethernet
broadcast address:

```text
ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
```

In Scapy, an Ethernet frame can be created with:

```python
from scapy.all import Ether

ethernet = Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")
```

Scapy uses the `/` operator to encapsulate one protocol inside another:

```python
packet = ethernet / ARP(pdst="192.168.153.10")
```

This represents:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ Ethernet                    │
│ dst = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff     │
│                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   │
│   │ ARP                 │   │
│   │                     │   │
│   │ Who has             │   │
│   │ 192.168.153.10?     │   │
│   └─────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

Inspect the complete packet:

```python
packet.show()
```

Notice that `/` does **not** mean division in this context. Scapy overloads the
operator to construct a protocol stack.

### Sending and Receiving Packets

Scapy provides several functions for sending packets.

Because we are working directly with Ethernet frames, we will use `srp()`:

```python
from scapy.all import srp

answered, unanswered = srp(
    packet,
    timeout=2,
    verbose=False
)
```

`srp()` means approximately:

```text
send and receive packets at Layer 2
```

and returns two collections:

```text
answered
unanswered
```

Each item in `answered` contains both:

```text
packet sent  →  packet received
```

For an ARP response, the received packet provides the information we need:

```python
for sent, received in answered:
    print(received.psrc)
    print(received.hwsrc)
```

where:

```text
psrc   → source protocol address → IPv4 address
hwsrc  → source hardware address → MAC address
```

::: {.callout-note title="Scapy and asyncio"}
The `srp()` function used here is a **blocking operation**.

Calling it from an `async` function does not automatically make it
asynchronous:

```python
async def discover():
    answered, unanswered = srp(...)
```

While `srp()` is running, the Python `asyncio` event loop cannot execute other
tasks.

For this exercise, this is not a problem. Scapy sends the ARP probes and
collects their responses as a single discovery operation:

```text
                    ARP discovery
                         │
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     host 1            host 2            host 3
       │                 │                 │
       └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                         ▼
                    ARP responses
```

We will therefore perform ARP discovery with Scapy first and then use
`asyncio` for the SNMP queries:

```text
        Scapy ARP discovery
               │
               ▼
       discovered hosts
               │
       ┌───────┼───────┐
       ▼       ▼       ▼
     host 1  host 2  host 3
       │       │       │
       └── concurrent ─┘
          SNMP queries
           (asyncio)
```

This also illustrates an important Python concept:

> `asyncio` provides concurrency only when the operations being called are
> asynchronous and yield control while they are waiting.
:::

### Discovering a Complete Subnet

Scapy also accepts a network in CIDR notation as the destination of an ARP
request.

For example:

```python
ARP(pdst="192.168.153.0/24")
```

represents ARP requests for the addresses in that subnet.

Therefore, the basic discovery operation can be constructed as:

```python
from scapy.all import ARP, Ether, srp

network = "192.168.153.0/24"

packet = (
    Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")
    / ARP(pdst=network)
)

answered, unanswered = srp(
    packet,
    timeout=2,
    verbose=False
)
```

## ARP Is Not the Only Discovery Mechanism

Network discovery does not rely on a single universal mechanism.

Depending on the network and the information available, management systems may
combine different sources such as:

```text
ARP / neighbour tables
ICMP probes
SNMP
LLDP/CDP
routing information
DHCP information
DNS
traffic observation
...
```

For example, ICMP Echo Requests can also be used to probe IP addresses:

```text
Manager                           Device

   │── ICMP Echo Request ────────>│
   │<── ICMP Echo Reply ──────────│
```

However:

::: {.callout-warning}
No response to an ICMP Echo Request does **not** necessarily mean that no
device exists at that address.

ICMP may be filtered while other protocols, including SNMP, remain reachable.
:::

being discovered are on the local laboratory network.

# Modifying Managed Objects: SNMP SET

Until now, all our SNMP operations have been **read operations**:

```text
GET / GETNEXT / WALK
        │
        ▼
Manager reads information from the agent
```

SNMP can also modify managed objects using the **SET** operation:

```text
Manager                         Agent
   │                              │
   │──── SET request ────────────>│
   │                              │
   │<─── RESPONSE ────────────────│
   │                              │
```

However, only objects defined as writable in their MIB can be modified.

Would you consider SNMPv2c appropriate for management traffic crossing an
untrusted network?
:::

## Monitoring vs Configuration

SNMP can therefore be used for both:

```text
                  SNMP
                   │
          ┌────────┴────────┐
          ▼                 ▼
        READ              WRITE
          │                 │
   GET / GETNEXT           SET
   GETBULK / WALK           │
          │                 ▼
          ▼             Configuration
      Monitoring
      Telemetry
```

In this course, our main use of SNMP will be **monitoring and telemetry**.

Modern network automation frequently uses other mechanisms for configuration,
while SNMP remains widely used for retrieving operational state and metrics.

Nevertheless, understanding SET is important because it demonstrates that the
SNMP management model was designed for both **monitoring and control**.

# Securing SNMP: SNMPv3

In the previous section, you captured an SNMPv2c SET operation.

The packet contained not only the object being modified and its new value, but
also the **community string** used to authorize the operation.

This creates an obvious security problem.

> If someone can capture the credential that allows us to modify the router,
> how can SNMP be used securely?

## The Problem with Community-Based SNMP

SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c use a **community string** as a simple access-control
mechanism.

Conceptually:

```text
             "public"
Manager ─────────────────► Agent
             GET

          "write-community"
Manager ─────────────────► Agent
             SET
```

The community identifies the access rights associated with the request.

However, the community itself is transmitted without encryption.

As you observed in the packet capture:

```text
Network observer
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SNMPv2c packet           │
│                          │
│ Community: public        │
│ PDU: GET                 │
│ OID: ...                 │
└──────────────────────────┘
```

and, even more critically:

```text
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SNMPv2c packet           │
│                          │
│ Community: ********      │
│ PDU: SET                 │
│ OID: sysLocation.0       │
│ Value: ...               │
└──────────────────────────┘
```

::: {.callout-question}
What could an attacker do after capturing a valid read-write community?

Would choosing a very long and random community string solve the packet-capture
problem? Why?
:::

# SNMPv3 Security Model

SNMPv3 introduces a different security model.

Instead of identifying access using only a community string, SNMPv3 can provide:

- **authentication** — verify who sent the message;
- **integrity** — detect whether the message was modified;
- **privacy** — encrypt the protected part of the SNMP message.

SNMPv3 defines three commonly used security levels:

| Security level | Authentication | Encryption |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| `noAuthNoPriv` | No | No |
| `authNoPriv` | Yes | No |
| `authPriv` | Yes | Yes |

The names can be read as:

```text
noAuthNoPriv
   │      │
   │      └── no privacy
   └───────── no authentication


authNoPriv
 │     │
 │     └───── no privacy
 └─────────── authentication


authPriv
 │   │
 │   └─────── privacy
 └─────────── authentication
```

::: {.callout-question}
Which security level would you choose for management traffic crossing an
untrusted network?

What information is still potentially visible when using `authNoPriv`?
:::

## Configuring an SNMPv3 User

Configure an SNMPv3 user on your MikroTik for this experiment.

Use:

```text

```

and the authentication and privacy credentials assigned for your laboratory
environment.

::: {.callout-warning}
Do not reuse personal passwords.

The credentials used in this exercise are laboratory credentials and should
only be used inside the CyberRange.
:::

Your configuration requires several pieces of information:

```text

    │
    ├── username
    │
    ├── authentication protocol
    │       └── authentication password
    │
    └── privacy protocol
            └── privacy password
```


Verify that SNMPv3 access is enabled before continuing.

Use the Net-SNMP command-line tools to retrieve:

```text
sysUpTime.0
```

using SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy.

The command has the following general structure:

```bash
snmpget -v3 \
  -l authPriv \
  -u <USERNAME> \
  -a <AUTH_PROTOCOL> \
  -A '<AUTH_PASSWORD>' \
  -x <PRIV_PROTOCOL> \
  -X '<PRIV_PASSWORD>' \
  <MIKROTIK_IP> \
  1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0
```

where:

```text
-v3   SNMP version 3
-l    security level
-u    username
-a    authentication protocol
-A    authentication password
-x    privacy protocol
-X    privacy password
```

::: {.callout-question}
Compare this command with the SNMPv2c equivalent:

```bash
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0
```

What information has replaced the community string?
:::

## Inspecting SNMPv3 on the Network

Capture the SNMPv3 GET request and its response.

Compare them with the SNMPv2c GET captured earlier.

Try to identify:

- the SNMP version;
- the SNMPv3 username;
- the authentication-related information;
- the encrypted portion of the message.

Then try to locate:

```text
sysUpTime.0
```

and its returned value in the packet capture.

::: {.callout-question}
Can you read the requested OID as easily as you could with SNMPv2c?

Can you read the returned value?

Can you find the authentication password in the packet?

Can you find the privacy password?

Can you find the SNMPv3 username?
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Encryption does not mean that the complete network packet becomes invisible.

An observer can still see information required to transport and process the
packet, such as IP addresses, UDP ports and some SNMPv3 metadata.

With `authPriv`, however, the protected SNMP scoped PDU is encrypted.
:::

## SNMPv3 with PySNMP

Create:

```text
get_v3.py
```

Modify one of your previous GET programs so that it retrieves:

```text

```

using SNMPv3 with `authPriv`.

In PySNMP, SNMPv3 user-based security is configured using `UsmUserData`
instead of `CommunityData`.

Conceptually:

```python

```

becomes:

```python

    username,
    authKey=...,
    privKey=...,
    authProtocol=...,
    privProtocol=...
)
```

Apart from the security configuration, how much of the SNMP operation has

```text
what we want to retrieve
```

```text

```
:::

# Comparing SNMPv2c and SNMPv3

You have now retrieved the same managed object using both SNMPv2c and SNMPv3.

| | SNMPv2c | SNMPv3 `authPriv` |
|---|---|---|

| Authentication | | |
| Message integrity | | |
| Encryption/privacy | | |
| Credential visible in capture | | |
| OID/value readable in capture | | |

::: {.callout-question}
If you were deploying a new network monitoring system today, which version
would you choose when the devices support it?

Why might SNMPv2c nevertheless still be encountered in real networks?

# What Have We Built?

At the beginning of this lab, we had only:


You have progressively implemented the basic functions of a network management
system:

```text
                    NETWORK
```

# Context

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) remains one of the most widely used
mechanisms for retrieving status and operational information from network devices.

In this lab, we will use a MikroTik router as the managed device and Python to
develop simple network management and monitoring tools.

The lab follows a progression similar to that used by real network management
platforms:

1. **Discover** which devices are present in the network.
2. **Identify** which devices can be managed using SNMP.
3. **Inspect** the information exposed by those devices.
4. **Explore** their interfaces and other objects available through their MIBs.
5. **Monitor** how selected network parameters evolve over time.

Throughout the lab, you will work directly from a Linux system and use both
command-line tools and Python scripts.

# Learning Objectives

After completing this lab, you should be able to:

- prepare a Python environment on Linux for developing simple network management
  tools;
- understand the relationship between **OIDs**, **MIBs**, scalar objects, and tables;
- perform SNMP queries using `GET`, `GETNEXT`, and `WALK`;
- interpret SNMP responses and the `VarBind` structures exchanged between manager
  and agent;
- modify managed objects using `SET` when permitted by the agent;
- automatically discover devices on a network and determine which of them provide
  SNMP management;
- retrieve and interpret the interface table of a network device;
- use SNMP counters to calculate traffic rates;
- develop a simple interface monitor using Python;
- understand the fundamental differences between SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3.

# Lab Environment

Each student has an individual laboratory environment accessible through the
CyberRange.

The lab will mainly use two systems:

- a **Debian container**, from which command-line tools and Python scripts will
  be executed;
- a **MikroTik router**, which will act as the SNMP agent and the network device
  being monitored.

The basic architecture is:

```text
┌──────────────────────┐
│      Debian CT       │
│                      │
│  Python / pysnmp     │
│  snmpget / snmpwalk  │
│  tcpdump             │
└──────────┬───────────┘
           │
           │ SNMP
           ▼
┌──────────────────────┐
│      MikroTik        │
│                      │
│     SNMP Agent       │
│       MIB-II         │
└──────────────────────┘
````

# Preparing the Environment

In previous labs, the programming environment and the required Python libraries
may have been provided preconfigured. In this course, you will prepare your own
working environment.

This is a common task when deploying network management and observability tools:
before collecting telemetry, you need a system from which to run them.

## Accessing the Debian Container

Connect to your **Debian container (d13-basic-153)** through the CyberRange and open a terminal.

Check the operating system and the installed Python version:

```bash

```

Throughout this lab, the Debian container will act as the **SNMP manager**, while
the MikroTik router will act as the **SNMP agent**.

::: {.callout-note}
### Manager and agent

An **SNMP manager** sends requests to managed devices and processes their
responses.

An **SNMP agent** runs on the managed device and provides access to the
management information exposed by that device.
:::

## Installing SNMP Command-Line Tools

# First Contact with SNMP

We now have the tools required to act as an SNMP manager. The next step is to

## Configuring the MikroTik SNMP Agent

| SNMP version | SNMPv2c |
| Community | `public` |
| Access | Read-only |

::: {.callout-warning}
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c communities are transmitted without encryption and should
not be considered secure authentication mechanisms.

We use SNMPv2c here because it allows us to focus first on the SNMP data model
and protocol operations. SNMPv3 will be introduced later in the lab.
:::

## Your First SNMP GET

Let's retrieve `sysDescr.0` from the MikroTik.

`sysDescr` belongs to the `system` group of MIB-II and contains a textual
description of the managed device.

Its numeric OID is:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

From the Debian container, execute:

```bash
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

You should obtain a response similar to:

```text
iso.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0 = STRING: ...
```

The exact value depends on your MikroTik router.

Notice that the result contains three different pieces of information:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0  =  STRING  :  value
        │                  │         │
        │                  │         └── Object value
        │                  │
        │                  └──────────── ASN.1 data type
        │
        └─────────────────────────────── Object identifier
```

This `(OID, value)` association is the basic information carried by an SNMP
**VarBind**.

::: {.callout-note}
### Why does the OID end in `.0`?

`sysDescr` is a scalar object.

SNMP identifies an **instance** of a scalar object by appending `.0` to the
object OID. Therefore, a GET request must use the complete instance OID:

```text
sysDescr.0
```

Later, when working with tables, the suffix will have a different meaning:
it will identify a particular row of the table.
:::

# GET Operations and VarBinds

In the previous section, you retrieved a single managed object using an SNMP
GET operation.

An SNMP GET request, however, can contain **more than one VarBind**. This allows
a manager to request several objects using a single SNMP message.

In this section, we will compare both approaches and examine how SNMP handles
errors.

## A Minimal PySNMP Example

PySNMP provides an asynchronous API based on Python's `asyncio`.

The following example retrieves `sysUpTime.0` from an SNMP agent:

```python
import asyncio

from pysnmp.hlapi.v3arch.asyncio import (
    SnmpEngine,
    CommunityData,
    UdpTransportTarget,
    ContextData,
    ObjectType,
    ObjectIdentity,
    get_cmd,
)


async def main():
    target = await UdpTransportTarget.create(
        ("<MIKROTIK_IP>", 161)
    )

    error_indication, error_status, error_index, var_binds = await get_cmd(
        SnmpEngine(),
        CommunityData("public", mpModel=1),
        target,
        ContextData(),
        ObjectType(ObjectIdentity("1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0")),
    )

    if error_indication:
        print(error_indication)
    elif error_status:
        print(
            f"{error_status.prettyPrint()} at "
            f"{error_index and var_binds[int(error_index) - 1][0] or '?'}"
        )
    else:
        for oid, value in var_binds:
            print("OID:  ", oid.prettyPrint())
            print("Type: ", type(value).__name__)
            print("Value:", value.prettyPrint())


asyncio.run(main())
```

Replace `<MIKROTIK_IP>` with the address of your MikroTik router and execute the
program.

Before continuing, identify in the program:

- where the requested OID is specified;
- where the program waits for the SNMP response;
- which variable contains the returned VarBinds.

## What Happens When an Object Does Not Exist?

We will now examine how SNMP handles errors.

Create a GET request containing several valid objects from the `system` group
and one OID that does not exist.

For example, you may deliberately modify one of the valid OIDs.

First perform the request using **SNMPv1**.


# Navigating the MIB: GETNEXT and WALK

So far, every GET operation required the manager to know the exact OID of the
object to retrieve.

But what happens if the manager does not know all the objects available below
a particular OID?

SNMP provides the `GETNEXT` operation for this purpose.

## Using GETNEXT

A GETNEXT request does not ask for the value of the specified OID itself.
Instead, it asks the agent for the **next OID in lexicographical order**.

For example, consider part of the MIB-II `system` subtree:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1
│
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0   sysDescr.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0   sysObjectID.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0   sysUpTime.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.4.0   sysContact.0
├── 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.5.0   sysName.0
└── ...
```

If the manager asks for the object following:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

the agent should return:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0
```

Try it from the command line:

```bash
snmpgetnext -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0
```

Now try:

```bash
snmpgetnext -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.2.0
```

and observe the returned OID.

of a MIB subtree?
:::

## Building a WALK from GETNEXT

There is no `WALK` PDU in the SNMP protocol.

An SNMP walk is obtained by repeatedly asking the agent for the next object:

```text
start OID
    │
    ▼
 GETNEXT
    │
    ▼
returned OID ───┐
                │
                ▼
             GETNEXT
                │
                ▼
          returned OID ───┐
                          │
                         ...
```

The OID returned by one request becomes the starting OID for the next request.

The process continues until the returned OID no longer belongs to the subtree
being explored.

# Working with SNMP Tables

Scalar objects such as `sysName.0` represent a single value.

Network management, however, frequently involves collections of similar
objects. A router may have many interfaces, routes, neighbours, or addresses.

SNMP represents this type of information using **tables**.

## The Interface Table

MIB-II provides information about the network interfaces of a device below the
`interfaces` subtree:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.2
```

Explore it:

```bash
snmpwalk -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> 1.3.6.1.2.1.2
```

The interface table contains information such as:

| Object | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ifIndex` | Interface identifier |
| `ifDescr` | Interface description |
| `ifType` | Interface type |
| `ifMtu` | Maximum transmission unit |
| `ifSpeed` | Estimated interface bandwidth |
| `ifPhysAddress` | Physical address |
| `ifAdminStatus` | Desired interface state |
| `ifOperStatus` | Current operational state |
| `ifInOctets` | Received octets |
| `ifOutOctets` | Transmitted octets |

Unlike scalar objects, table objects have an **index** identifying the row.

For example:

```text
ifDescr.1 = "ether1"
ifDescr.2 = "ether2"
ifDescr.3 = "ether3"
```

can be understood as:

```text
             ifIndex

               1        2        3
               │        │        │
               ▼        ▼        ▼

ifDescr      ether1   ether2   ether3
ifType       ...      ...      ...
ifSpeed      ...      ...      ...
ifOperStatus ...      ...      ...
ifInOctets   ...      ...      ...
ifOutOctets  ...      ...      ...
```

The index therefore connects values belonging to the **same interface**.

# From Counters to Telemetry

In the previous section, you observed that `ifInOctets` and `ifOutOctets` are
**cumulative counters**.

They do not directly tell us the current traffic rate of an interface.

To obtain a rate, the manager must sample a counter at different times and
calculate how much it has changed.

## From a Counter to a Rate

Suppose that the value of `ifInOctets` is measured at two different times:

| Time | Counter |
|---|---:|
| $t_1$ | $C_1$ |
| $t_2$ | $C_2$ |

The average incoming traffic rate during that interval is:

$$
R_{\text{in}} =
8 \frac{C_2-C_1}{t_2-t_1}
$$

where:

- $C_1$ and $C_2$ are counter values in octets;
- $t_1$ and $t_2$ are measured in seconds;
- the factor 8 converts octets into bits;
- $R_{\text{in}}$ is expressed in bit/s.

The same calculation can be applied to `ifOutOctets`.

::: {.callout-important}
SNMP does not calculate the traffic rate for us.

The agent exposes a **counter**. The manager samples that counter and derives
the **rate**.

This distinction between a raw measurement and a derived metric is fundamental
in network monitoring and observability.
:::

## Counter Size Matters

The original MIB-II interface table defines:

```text
ifInOctets
ifOutOctets
```

as 32-bit counters.

A 32-bit unsigned counter can represent values from:

$$
0
\quad\text{to}\quad
2^{32}-1
$$

After reaching its maximum value, the counter wraps around.

Consider a continuously busy **1 Gbit/s** interface.

::: {.callout-question}
Calculate approximately how long it would take a 32-bit octet counter to wrap
around at 1 Gbit/s.

5 minutes?
:::

For higher-capacity interfaces, IF-MIB provides 64-bit counters:

```text
ifHCInOctets
ifHCOutOctets
```

where **HC** stands for *High Capacity*.

Whenever they are available, these counters are generally preferable for
traffic monitoring.

::: {.callout-note}
A robust monitoring application should not simply assume that:

```text
new_counter >= old_counter
```

A counter may become smaller because of:

- counter wraparound;
- device or interface restart;
- agent restart.

Production monitoring systems must account for these situations.
:::

# Automatic Device Discovery

Until now, we have assumed that the network manager already knows the IP
address of the device to monitor.

In a real network management system, this information may not be known in
advance. Management platforms therefore provide **device discovery** mechanisms
to find devices and build an inventory automatically.

A simplified discovery process can be represented as:

```text
          Network
             │
             ▼
      Discover hosts
             │
             ▼
       IP + MAC address
             │
             ▼
        Probe SNMP
             │
        ┌────┴────┐
        │         │
       No        Yes
                  │
                  ▼
             Identify device
                  │
                  ▼
       sysName / sysDescr /
          sysObjectID
                  │
                  ▼
          Device inventory
```

In this section, you will implement a simplified version of this process.

## Discovering Hosts on a Local Network

If the manager is directly connected to an IPv4 LAN, **ARP** provides a useful
mechanism for discovering active hosts.

The manager can send an ARP request asking:

```text
Who has 192.168.153.1?
Who has 192.168.153.2?
Who has 192.168.153.3?
...
```

A device using one of those addresses can reply with its MAC address:

```text
Manager                                  Device

   │                                       │
   │── ARP: Who has 192.168.153.10? ─────>│
   │                                       │
   │<── ARP: 192.168.153.10 is at MAC ────│
   │                                       │
```

This provides two useful pieces of inventory information:

```text
IP address  ↔  MAC address
```

::: {.callout-note}
ARP discovery only works for devices in the same Layer-2 broadcast domain.

Routers do not normally forward ARP requests. Therefore, a management platform
cannot use ARP alone to discover arbitrary remote networks.
:::

### Ethernet and ARP

ARP requests are transmitted inside Ethernet frames.

An ARP request intended for all hosts on the LAN therefore uses the Ethernet
broadcast address:

```text
ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
```

In Scapy, an Ethernet frame can be created with:

```python
from scapy.all import Ether

ethernet = Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")
```

Scapy uses the `/` operator to encapsulate one protocol inside another:

```python
packet = ethernet / ARP(pdst="192.168.153.10")
```

This represents:

```text
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ Ethernet                    │
│ dst = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff     │
│                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   │
│   │ ARP                 │   │
│   │                     │   │
│   │ Who has             │   │
│   │ 192.168.153.10?     │   │
│   └─────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

Inspect the complete packet:

```python
packet.show()
```

Notice that `/` does **not** mean division in this context. Scapy overloads the
operator to construct a protocol stack.

### Sending and Receiving Packets

Scapy provides several functions for sending packets.

Because we are working directly with Ethernet frames, we will use `srp()`:

```python
from scapy.all import srp

answered, unanswered = srp(
    packet,
    timeout=2,
    verbose=False
)
```

`srp()` means approximately:

```text
send and receive packets at Layer 2
```

and returns two collections:

```text
answered
unanswered
```

Each item in `answered` contains both:

```text
packet sent  →  packet received
```

For an ARP response, the received packet provides the information we need:

```python
for sent, received in answered:
    print(received.psrc)
    print(received.hwsrc)
```

where:

```text
psrc   → source protocol address → IPv4 address
hwsrc  → source hardware address → MAC address
```

::: {.callout-note title="Scapy and asyncio"}
The `srp()` function used here is a **blocking operation**.

Calling it from an `async` function does not automatically make it
asynchronous:

```python
async def discover():
    answered, unanswered = srp(...)
```

While `srp()` is running, the Python `asyncio` event loop cannot execute other
tasks.

For this exercise, this is not a problem. Scapy sends the ARP probes and
collects their responses as a single discovery operation:

```text
                    ARP discovery
                         │
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     host 1            host 2            host 3
       │                 │                 │
       └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                         ▼
                    ARP responses
```

We will therefore perform ARP discovery with Scapy first and then use
`asyncio` for the SNMP queries:

```text
        Scapy ARP discovery
               │
               ▼
       discovered hosts
               │
       ┌───────┼───────┐
       ▼       ▼       ▼
     host 1  host 2  host 3
       │       │       │
       └── concurrent ─┘
          SNMP queries
           (asyncio)
```

This also illustrates an important Python concept:

> `asyncio` provides concurrency only when the operations being called are
> asynchronous and yield control while they are waiting.
:::

## ARP Is Not the Only Discovery Mechanism

Network discovery does not rely on a single universal mechanism.

Depending on the network and the information available, management systems may
combine different sources such as:

```text
ARP / neighbour tables
ICMP probes
SNMP
LLDP/CDP
routing information
DHCP information
DNS
traffic observation
...
```

For example, ICMP Echo Requests can also be used to probe IP addresses:

```text
Manager                           Device

   │── ICMP Echo Request ────────>│
   │<── ICMP Echo Reply ──────────│
```

However:

::: {.callout-warning}
No response to an ICMP Echo Request does **not** necessarily mean that no
device exists at that address.

ICMP may be filtered while other protocols, including SNMP, remain reachable.
:::

For this lab, **ARP will be used for initial discovery** because the devices
being discovered are on the local laboratory network.

## Why Sequential Discovery Does Not Scale

Suppose several devices have been discovered:

```text

192.168.153.2
192.168.153.3
...
```

A sequential SNMP probe behaves approximately as:

```text
Device 1: request ───── wait ───── response
                                     │
Device 2:                            request ───── wait ───── response
                                                                  │
Device 3:                                                         ...
```

This becomes particularly inefficient when a device does **not** respond.

The manager must wait for the SNMP timeout before moving to the next device.

::: {.callout-question}

of them responds?

:::

# Modifying Managed Objects: SNMP SET

Until now, all our SNMP operations have been **read operations**:

```text
GET / GETNEXT / WALK
        │
        ▼
Manager reads information from the agent
```

SNMP can also modify managed objects using the **SET** operation:

```text
Manager                         Agent
   │                              │
   │──── SET request ────────────>│
   │                              │
   │<─── RESPONSE ────────────────│
   │                              │
```

However, only objects defined as writable in their MIB can be modified.

## Read and Write Access

For the previous exercises, the MikroTik SNMP agent was configured with a
read-only community:

```text
public
```

This is sufficient for monitoring, but it should not allow configuration
changes.

Try to modify `sysLocation.0` using the read-only community.

For example, with the Net-SNMP command-line tools:

```bash
snmpset -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> \
  1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0 s "Network Management Lab"
```

Here:

```text
1.3.6.1.2.1.1.6.0    → sysLocation.0
s                      → OCTET STRING
"Network Management Lab" → new value
```

Observe the result.

::: {.callout-question}
Was the operation accepted?

Why should a community used by a monitoring system normally have read-only
access?
:::

## Enabling Write Access

Configure a **separate SNMP community** on the MikroTik with write access.

Do not modify the read-only `public` community.

Use the write community only for this part of the lab.

::: {.callout-warning}
A read-write SNMP community provides the ability to modify writable managed
objects on the device.

It should therefore not be used for routine monitoring.
:::

Repeat the SET operation using the write community.

Then verify the result independently with a GET:

```bash
snmpget -v2c -c public <MIKROTIK_IP> \

```

The complete operation is therefore:

```text
       write community                 read community

Manager ─────── SET ───────► Agent ◄────── GET ─────── Manager
              │                │
              │                ▼
              │          sysLocation.0
              │                │
              └── changes ─────┘
```

::: {.callout-question}
Why is it useful to verify the result using a separate GET rather than assuming
that the configuration has changed because a SET request was sent?
:::

## Monitoring vs Configuration

SNMP can therefore be used for both:

```text
                  SNMP
                   │
          ┌────────┴────────┐
          ▼                 ▼
        READ              WRITE
          │                 │
   GET / GETNEXT           SET
   GETBULK / WALK           │
          │                 ▼
          ▼             Configuration
      Monitoring
      Telemetry
```

In this course, our main use of SNMP will be **monitoring and telemetry**.

Modern network automation frequently uses other mechanisms for configuration,
while SNMP remains widely used for retrieving operational state and metrics.

Nevertheless, understanding SET is important because it demonstrates that the
SNMP management model was designed for both **monitoring and control**.

# Securing SNMP: SNMPv3

In the previous section, you captured an SNMPv2c SET operation.

The packet contained not only the object being modified and its new value, but
also the **community string** used to authorize the operation.

This creates an obvious security problem.

> If someone can capture the credential that allows us to modify the router,
> how can SNMP be used securely?

## The Problem with Community-Based SNMP

SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c use a **community string** as a simple access-control
mechanism.

Conceptually:

```text
             "public"
Manager ─────────────────► Agent
             GET

          "write-community"
Manager ─────────────────► Agent
             SET
```

The community identifies the access rights associated with the request.

However, the community itself is transmitted without encryption.

As you observed in the packet capture:

```text
Network observer
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SNMPv2c packet           │
│                          │
│ Community: public        │
│ PDU: GET                 │
│ OID: ...                 │
└──────────────────────────┘
```

and, even more critically:

```text
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ SNMPv2c packet           │
│                          │
│ Community: ********      │
│ PDU: SET                 │
│ OID: sysLocation.0       │
│ Value: ...               │
└──────────────────────────┘
```

::: {.callout-question}
What could an attacker do after capturing a valid read-write community?

Would choosing a very long and random community string solve the packet-capture
problem? Why?
:::

# SNMPv3 Security Model

SNMPv3 introduces a different security model.

Instead of identifying access using only a community string, SNMPv3 can provide:

- **authentication** — verify who sent the message;
- **integrity** — detect whether the message was modified;
- **privacy** — encrypt the protected part of the SNMP message.

SNMPv3 defines three commonly used security levels:

| Security level | Authentication | Encryption |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| `noAuthNoPriv` | No | No |
| `authNoPriv` | Yes | No |
| `authPriv` | Yes | Yes |

The names can be read as:

```text
noAuthNoPriv
   │      │
   │      └── no privacy
   └───────── no authentication


authNoPriv
 │     │
 │     └───── no privacy
 └─────────── authentication


authPriv
 │   │
 │   └─────── privacy
 └─────────── authentication
```

::: {.callout-question}
Which security level would you choose for management traffic crossing an
untrusted network?

What information is still potentially visible when using `authNoPriv`?
:::

```bash

  -a <AUTH_PROTOCOL> \
  -A '<AUTH_PASSWORD>' \
  -x <PRIV_PROTOCOL> \
```

```text
-l    security level
-u    username
-a    authentication protocol
-A    authentication password
-x    privacy protocol
-X    privacy password
```
